title: RESTORING AMERICA'S INDUSTRIAL BASE: THE ROLE OF SMALL BUSINESSES IN NATIONAL SECURITY
text: Good morning, Chairman Williams, Ranking Member Cisneros, and Members of the Committee. My name is Angela Dingle. I am president and CEO of Women Impacting Public Policy, a national nonpartisan organization advocating on behalf of women-owned businesses. I am also a small business owner with more than 20 years of experience in the federal marketplace, helping companies navigate it successfully. Thank you for the opportunity to testify. This hearing asks the right questions. Small businesses are not bystanders to America's industrial base. They are its foundation. A procurement system built on a broad base of small firms is more competitive, more resilient, and harder for our adversaries to disrupt. A narrow one built up around a smaller pool of larger contractors is a national security risk. And yet that base is shrinking. In fiscal year 2024, agencies awarded a record $183 billion in prime contracts to small businesses, the highest total ever. But the number of firms doing that work has been cut nearly in half from roughly 121,000 in 2009 to about 63,000 in 2022. Record dollars are flowing to fewer and fewer companies. As firms leave, agencies grow more dependent on a smaller group of large incumbents, reducing competition, raising costs, and weakening the government's own leverage. It is the opposite of a strong industrial base. What is driving small businesses out? In a word, unpredictability. As a business owner, I factor risk into every decision: how I spend my time, how I price, whether to pursue an opportunity at all. I need real confidence that I have a chance at winning to justify the investment. When contracts are awarded and then abruptly canceled, when policy shifts without warning, that confidence erodes and small firms simply walk away. Stability and predictability are not luxuries. They are conditions that keep us in the market and investing in the capacity this country needs. This is why the Rule of Two matters so much. It has long been a bedrock protection for small businesses, and any threat to it, even a potential one, raises risk and accelerates consolidation. Congress should retain and codify the Rule of Two as a true shall requirement applied consistently across contract vehicles. WIPP is proud to support the Protecting Small Business Competition Act of 2025, which does just that. We commend the Committee for its unanimous approval of this bill and hope that the full House will follow your lead. I now want to talk about a program that is near to our mission at WIPP, the Women-Owned Small Business, or WOSB, Program. The WOSB Program and similar programs are not handouts, nor are they charity. They exist to level a field that is not yet level and to give the government the widest possible pool of qualified competitors, and they work. In fiscal year 2024, women-owned small businesses won $31.7 billion in federal contracts, and the certified WOSB Program grew to more than 13,400 firms. Women-owned firms are winning contracts and delivering, but only when they get a fair shot to compete. That is good business and good government. A few practical points. Subcontracting and the chance to grow into a prime is how small firms become the durable suppliers the industrial base relies on. Both deserve protection. And the offices meant to champion us inside agencies, the OSDBUs, are understaffed or vacant. As the administration reexamines federal programs, the wide reach of those reviews has inadvertently captured offices and resources that are vital to small firms. Even though supporting small business is squarely a competition and capacity issue, not a peripheral one, a program is only as strong as the people charged with making it work. Small businesses are not just beneficiaries of federal contracts. We are essential partners in this nation's security and prosperity. We bring the innovation, agility, and cost savings that lead the government to meet its mission quickly and effectively. Protect and expand our role, and you strengthen the industrial base. But if we keep facing instability and a shrinking chance to compete, you should not be surprised when fewer of us remain. Thank you, and I look forward to answering any of your questions. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentlelady yields back. Thank you. We will now move to the Member questions under the 5-minute rule. I recognize myself for 5 minutes. Mr. Schwartz, the number of contractors supporting the defense industrial base has shrunk by roughly 40 percent since 2010. Rising regulatory costs were cited as a major reason small businesses are leaving these federal contracting programs. For small firms, every dollar spent on compliance is a dollar not spent on innovation or production or workforce or even cybersecurity. So the question will be, how has the Trump administration's revolutionary FAR overhaul addressed that challenge? Mr. SCHWARTZ. Thank you. So, in a bumper sticker, I would say one of the ways to improve acquisition generally, and for small businesses as well, is fewer regulations, more consistently enforced by an empowered workforce. And this effort to rewrite the FAR and then the DFAR, the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation, strikes at two of those. By deregulating, like we have talked about, like we have all talked about, it gives small businesses more opportunity to focus on the business of what they are delivering instead of non-added valuate, non-added regulation and compliance. That is one. But the second thing, which might be the even more important impact that people don't necessarily think about, is the message we are sending to the workforce. The message we are sending is less about compliance and more about doing the right thing and empowering them. And I am hopeful that this rewrite is really going to send that message because unless we deal with the workforce, almost everything else is playing around the margins. Chairman WILLIAMS. All right. Thank you. Mr. Jaworowski, as the national security landscape becomes increasingly shaped by cutting-edge software and artificial intelligence, the defense industrial base is under pressure to modernize faster than traditional acquisition process was designed to support. So the question is, from your position leading Infinity Systems Engineering, how do you see the role of a small business evolving over the next decade, and what structural changes are most necessary for the defense industrial base to fully leverage main street's capabilities? Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Thank you for the question, Mr. Chairman. I think that the recent extension of the Small Business Innovative Research Program is going to go a long way to help satisfy some of that gap that exists, particularly when it comes to AI. AI is something--that is an area that we operate. We are active in the SBIR Program. I would love to see it become permanent, not just a 5-year extension so that we don't have another lapse like we did recently. But that program is very, very encouraging for new entrants to this market to come in and participate. There are a lot of companies out there that don't participate in the defense industrial base that can absolutely bring capability that is well needed, and that program is really the way to do it. Chairman WILLIAMS. Okay. Thank you. In the limited time I got, Mr. Closson, Colossal Contracting's identity as a veteran-owned business speaks to something larger happening across the federal landscape, and it represents the growing recognition that smaller companies can often move faster and more effectively, stay closer to the mission needs of government customers. So my question is, in an environment where agencies are looking for partners who are even--who can rapidly integrate emerging technologies and adapt to changing requirements, how does Colossal Contracting leverage its veteran-led mindset and small business agility as a competitive advantage? Mr. CLOSSON. Thank you, sir. Being agile, right? Being aggressive. I mean, that is part of who we are and what we are trained to be as veterans. That is why I think it is great to see so many veterans going into the entrepreneurial, you know, mindset and to becoming service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses. That value that we are trained with and the ethics that we have and the drive from being military have delivered absolute value. And especially in supporting the defense industrial bases, you know, a lot of us veterans are dealing with the missions that we dealt with when we served. So we are able to see what the issues are, understand their mission, and do what we can to elevate it. And because we are not massive, we don't have these huge layers, right, we are dealing directly with the program, with people that understand the mission. And what we are doing is we are taking all the different types of technologies as an IT VAR and as a master aggregator and bringing those together to answer the mail and to elevate their solution, so--and to elevate their mission. So, you know, to answer, sir, is who we were trained to be is delivering absolute max value. And I believe it will continue to do that. Chairman WILLIAMS. All right, thank you. The gentleman yields back. I now recognize the Ranking Member for 5 minutes of questions. Mr. CISNEROS. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Ms. Dingle, with the administration's ongoing attack on the 8(a) and legislation to eliminate the women-owned small business programs pending, can you reiterate for the Committee the value of the SBA's programs not only for small businesses, but for the government and the industrial base? Ms. DINGLE. Thank you, Ranking Member. The Women-Owned Small Business Program and the SBA programs like the 8(a) Program--the 8(a) in particular is a business development program, and the Women-Owned Small Business Program--they create a level playing field. They are not handouts. For every contract that I have ever won, I had to compete for those contracts, and so do the other businesses. When, as my colleague here mentioned in his comments, when we have to compete against multibillion-dollar firms who have existed for hundreds of years, it is more costly. It creates an unpredictable environment that we are not able to determine whether or not we should invest the dollars that are necessary. And it makes it really hard for business owners to be able to grow. One contract award in one of those programs can be a gamechanger. It can completely change the trajectory of the company because we simply need a foot in the door, and these programs create those opportunities for you to get a foot in the door. Mr. CISNEROS. Yeah. You know, a company like General Dynamics, right, did not start out as a big corporation. It started out with kind of doing a small company doing a contract for NASA, and, and we need to have those game-changers out there. But halfway through this fiscal year, Ms. Dingle, documents circulated online showing SBA changed their scorecard criteria and lowered each agency's spending targets. What will be the impact of SBA telling agencies they should spend less, potentially $12 billion less on small business? Ms. DINGLE. I think it just flies in the face of what this Committee and this conversation that we are having. If we continue to say that small businesses are the engine of the U.S. economy, then we have to create an opportunity for those small businesses to compete. One of my other colleagues mentioned the burden that is on the contracting officers. Some of these programs assist them in getting their work done. And sometimes they just need an easy button. They will take the least path of resistance. And so if you say to an agency, you only have to spend $12 billion less than you did, they will simply do that and small businesses will be cut out. Ultimately, for the government, that means less innovation. It means less competition, and it means additional cost because we believe, and I am certain my colleagues would agree with me, that small businesses can do it cheaper and faster and with more flexibility. Mr. CISNEROS. Thank you very much for that answer. Mr. Closson, the FAR rewrite removes the justification and approval requirements for direct awards when agencies utilize the Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Businesses or other small business programs. Will these changes make it easier to provide contracting opportunities to serve disabled veteranowned businesses? Mr. CLOSSON. Thank you, sir. I believe so. I believe removing the J&A requirements and getting contracting officers also comfortable with doing sole sources. The sole source has been around for a while for the SDVOSBs, but not many people use it. Contracting officers see it as difficult. They don't want to have to justify things. So we are hoping that that mixed with the Rule of Two is really going to open up some things and be able to showcase the service-disabled veteranowned small businesses out there and be able to provide that max value. So to answer, sir, absolutely, I think that it will, hopefully, open up some more solid SDVOSBs to doing sole source work, and that mixed with the Rule of Two, it should open things up. Mr. CISNEROS. Since you mentioned the Rule of Two, let me ask you this. Can you quickly address what a sunset of the Rule of Two would mean for small business participation in the industrial base? Mr. CLOSSON. It would hurt. If that went away and contracting officers and program people were not evaluating the value of small business, I think it would impact us greatly. I mean, we need the Rule of Two. We need there to be that first look, especially, hey, there is the place for the systems integrator where they are working on massive programs that protect this nation, and I am good with that. And we work with a lot of them. But there is a lot of amazing opportunities for the agility and the expertise that small businesses bring, and we need that Rule of Two. Mr. CISNEROS. All right. Ms. Dingle, since you mentioned the Rule of Two, in our last 30 seconds here, can you answer that same question. What would it mean if this sunsetted? Ms. DINGLE. I agree. I mean, it would just be disastrous for small businesses. That Rule of Two helps me in my decisionmaking as a business owner when I am evaluating whether or not I am going to compete on an opportunity. The Rule of Two makes it something that is viable for me to consider for competition. And the predictability of knowing what is going to happen in this environment is what makes me decide whether or not I am going to continue to do business in the federal marketplace. Mr. CISNEROS. All right. Well, thank you for your testimony, and I yield back. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentleman yields back. I now recognize Mr. Alford from the great state of Missouri for 5 minutes. Mr. ALFORD. Well, thank you, Mr. Chair. I am also on the Appropriations Committee, and we have two markups across the hall, so I am kind of back and forth. But I did not get to listen to your testimony, but I did read it, and I am high on the end there. I am excited that you are here today so thanks for coming here. When most people think about our national defense, they think about large defense contractors, but behind every major weapon system, aircraft, and military platform is a network of small businesses providing innovative technology, specialized manufacturing, and critical supply chain support. Small businesses are essential to maintaining America's technological edge, and they are often the first to deploy emerging capabilities in areas like artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, and electronic warfare, and they also provide the competition and innovation necessary to make sure that our military has access to the best capabilities available. However, despite their importance, the number of small businesses participating in federal contracting has declined significantly, raising concerns about consolidation within the defense industrial base and long-term resilience. And as we face increasing competition from adversaries such as China, it is critical that we expand opportunities for innovative American companies to enter and succeed in the defense marketplace. Today's hearing provides an opportunity to better understand those challenges and identify ways Congress can strengthen small business participation in our defense industrial base. I represent a great base in the DOD family, Fort Leonard Wood. We also have Whiteman Air Force Base, but we have exciting things going on. We have a technology park, 10 square miles on the base in Fort Leonard Wood in the southeastern part of our district, where we are trying to attract more small defense capabilities there. So Mr. Jaworowski, did I pronounce that correct? Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Very close. Mr. ALFORD. All right, very close. Jaworowski, better? All right. Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Better. Mr. ALFORD. Your business started out contracting with DOD and then won an SBIR award. What led you and your company to pursue that award after receiving multiple defense contracts? Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Thank you for your question, sir. We--you know, you hit the nail on the head at the beginning of your statement and question there. You know, Infinity has been around for 30 years, but we were founded on subcontracts with the large primes. So some of those large primes today are still some of our biggest customers. We are primarily a services company providing engineering services to those primes and to DOW on the satellite operations front. About 5 years ago, we made the decision that we were seeking out some higher margin work. We didn't really want to leave DOD and go into the commercial space, and we saw SBIR as an opportunity to bring some ideas and innovations to the table that we saw we saw as gaps with some of the large primes that were probably not meaty enough for them to go after themselves, but they were difference-making enough for us that we were able to innovate and capitalize on that program, and it has been a game-changer for us. Mr. ALFORD. Mr. Schwartz, as you know, Secretary Hegseth proposed a $1.5 trillion defense budget for fiscal year. We are going to be taking up the defense appropriations in the coming weeks right across the hall. How can Congress make sure that small businesses are positioned to compete for these dollars? Mr. SCHWARTZ. That is a great question. I think there are a lot of examples. There are a lot of things that Congress can do to help small businesses have a level playing field, and I will just reiterate two of them. One is when a company loses an SBIR, right, they don't necessarily get the feedback that would help them do a better bid next time, right? Now, this actually, because GAO bid protests had been mentioned, this was a problem with bid protests where companies didn't know why they were losing bid protests. So Congress actually legislated and said, DOD, you will do enhanced debriefings, and they did. And companies thought that was very helpful. And in fact, my understanding is the data said that bid protests decreased because companies understood. That is one thing that Congress could do. They could say you shall give better debriefings for SBIRs, you know, so companies know how to compete better. And another one very quickly is shared SCIF space. Companies don't always have the investment if they are small businesses to invest in that, which means they can't compete for the bid---Mr. ALFORD. Right. Mr. SCHWARTZ.--and then they can't perform. Excess SCIF space in GSA, for example, is a great way, like, for a pay-forfee like a WeWorks---Mr. ALFORD. Right. Mr. SCHWARTZ.--is another opportunity. Mr. ALFORD. Well, two very innovative ideas. I think we had similar legislation with other government contracts that passed through this Committee and the full House, I believe, that required the government to give explanations to small businesses of why they did not secure a contract. And I think maybe this would be good to look at this in this case and also the shared SCIF space. Great ideas. We will get to work on that. I yield back. Thank you. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentleman yields back. I now recognize Ms. Goodlander from the great state of New Hampshire for 5 minutes. Ms. GOODLANDER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you to our witnesses for being here today for this really important hearing. I want to start with two numbers that have come up in this hearing: 51 to 5. Fifty-one to five. That is how many prime defense contractors we had in this country in 1993, 51. Just 7 years later, we were down to 5. And this was driven by consolidation that the Pentagon itself blessed. You know, fast forward to today, we are seeing this same movie once again, even more consolidation. And Mr. Jaworowski, I want to be sure to emphasize this very powerful portion of your written testimony where you described the second Valley of Death, this frozen middle where small businesses like yours are trapped with three really challenging options. The first, and I applaud you for pursuing it, to continue to try to operate in this environment where the deck is stacked against you, the rules are not written for you. And I want to work with you and each one of our witnesses who are here today to help us write better rules of the road. When I think of President Eisenhower, General Eisenhower, Mr. Schwartz, you invoked him, I think he would be very disappointed in the progress that we have made since 1953. We have reversed course from where we should be. And I came to Congress having worked in the Antitrust Division at the Justice Department ,where we worked really hard to dust off the federal code to give and empower people across our administration, including in the Pentagon, the confidence that they can enforce the rules that we have on the books. And I am here now and I want to write better rules of the road that are going to help businesses trapped in the second Valley of Death. The three options you have in front of you, can you just say a bit more about the two other bad options that are available to a small business like yours, sir, in the second Valley of Death? Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Sure, I am happy to. You know, really selling out is what we are seeing most prevalent. Most companies are getting to our size and they find that this competitive landscape has changed and it gets frustrating and it is the easy answer is to just take the exit. Ms. GOODLANDER. Sell to a prime. Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Sell to a prime or sell to private equity. Private equity is what we see more commonly and they are consolidating small businesses like ours, ultimately for a sale of that entity to probably to a prime in a more strategic transaction. The second road is really to say, we are going to go try to acquire another company ourselves. And that is capital intensive. Ms. GOODLANDER. Yeah. Mr. JAWOROWSKI. And that is a really, really challenging decision to make for an independent, privately held company. And if--the capital is just not there to do something like that. So we would have to take on an outside investment, and when we do that, you are probably going to lose some control over your company, and we are not interested in doing that either. Ms. GOODLANDER. Well, I appreciate that. Mr. Closson, can you speak to--I gather you are also riding through the second Valley of Death. Mr. CLOSSON. Yes, I am. You know, we are on that, in our world as an IT VAR, as soon as you go over 150, you are now competing against systems integrators and very large companies. If you walk into Colossal's headquarters today, you will hear music playing, people, you know, enjoying life, but it has a small business feel, right? It is a culture that we created that we will lose, right? If we can't compete, because as soon as we go over 151, without things like the gentleman was saying here, losing who you are, selling out to private equity, you know, making a massive investment that you don't have, right, you are going to lose who you are. I said the other day to our group that I wish and I hope and I will work as hard as I can that Colossal becomes a legacy company and that we can stay around for a long time. But like I mentioned, I--my fear is I am constantly battling this under 150. And because we are an IT VAR, people will see that we are selling a lot of equipment with our services and look at us and say, hey, well, you are a large business, right? Ms. GOODLANDER. Right. Obviously, that barrier to enter the marketplace shouldn't be impeded by unnecessary paperwork. Is there anything tangible that we can be doing in Congress to simplify the process? Mr. SCHWARTZ. Yes, there are a couple of things, but one is there are a lot of regulations that stem from statute. So if you look at the Federal Acquisition Regulation overhaul that is being done right now, the revolutionary overhaul, what they are trying--what they are doing is taking everything that is not required by statute and taking it out, right? But there are things that are required by statute that have been required by statute because of things that are 20, 30 years old that perhaps we have not reviewed of late that are still in there that is not being reviewed because of this overhaul, because the administration has no authority to take that out, or any of the agencies. So one thing that could be done is a systematic review of the statutory requirements and regulation with a very simple question: is this doing more good than harm? Right? Because some of those--there used to be a regulation that said you had to use dollar coins in every vending machine on a base. That was ultimately appealed because of something that Congress did, or there was a requirement you had to use double-sided paper. Right? Those might be requirements that are examples that we may want to start reviewing those and getting rid of those so we can focus on the important things. So that would be at the top of my list. Mr. BRESNAHAN. Well, the 11 words you never want to hear: we are from the government and we are here to help. So, honestly. My second question for Mr. Closson. First of all, thank you for your service. As the founder of the Service Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business, what advice would you have or to give to a veteran in the early stages of starting a small business? And this is something that I frequently encounter when I am meeting with my constituents. They served our country, and sometimes it is incredibly frustrating to get that inertia moving to be able to get the business off of the ground. So if you can maybe identify perhaps one or two key suggestions that I can take back to them. Mr. CLOSSON. First is find a good program. Like the DAV has programs where they have mentorship programs for starting small businesses. It is one of the best ones I have ever seen. I have been honored enough to teach a couple of those sessions. Extremely valuable for me. I actually sit through some of the others to get value. Extremely valuable. So the DAV puts on an awesome SDVOSB Entrepreneurial Veteran clinic for people starting business. Two is understanding how to monetize who you are and the value that you have. Being able to take that step, to dig into your Rolodex of people you have worked with in government or not and be able to monetize your relationships and bring value to their mission. Understand your value and how you can impact theirs. Mr. BRESNAHAN. Thank you for your service as well. And Mr. Chairman, I yield. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentleman yields back. I now recognize Ms. Scholten from the great state of Michigan for 5 minutes. Ms. SCHOLTEN. Thank you so much, Mr. Chairman and Mr. Ranking Member, and thank you for our witnesses for being here today. This is a really, really important conversation. You know, there is a through line here, right, that we agree small businesses are the backbone of our economy and they are foundational to the strength of our defense industrial base. On that, we agree. However, according to a 2022 study, the number of small businesses competing for awards through the Department of Defense dropped by 23 percent. Over that same time period, the number of firms that were awarded small-dollar contracts, less than $1 million, shrank by even more, by 32 percent. Ms. Dingle, what steps can we take to ensure that there are sufficient opportunities for small businesses who compete for these lower awards? Ms. DINGLE. Thank you for the question. I think we have heard from a number of my colleagues here about the Rule of Two creating opportunities, right, because that sets aside some of the business. But the other thing is consolidations right now are causing problems for us, some of the consolidations. And again, when you look at it from a taxpayer standpoint, it makes sense, but when you look at it from a business standpoint, that just takes some small businesses out of competition completely. You have got to be at a certain dollar figure to even be able to compete. So making small business set-asides available, using tools like the Rule of Two, making sure that contracts are not necessarily consolidated. I will try to be sensitive to time, but as a small business owner who has worked in defense, we had existing incumbent work that was then moved to a consolidated contract vehicle that we weren't eligible to compete on. So even though we had gotten our foot in the door, now the door was--we were put on the outside of the door and the door was closed so we couldn't get back in. Ms. SCHOLTEN. Yeah. Ms. DINGLE. And so being mindful of those kind of things is something that is going to be important. Ms. SCHOLTEN. Yeah. Another factor that you have emphasized in your testimony is the ever-changing economic landscape and the instability. I mean, I know defense contracting or not, that is the number one issue that I hear about from our small businesses back home. A recent op-ed from WIPP emphasizes that the use of AI in small business operations presents both a critical opportunity and a barrier to entry for certain entrepreneurs. My bill, the AI-WISE Act, would address this challenge by requiring the SBA to create learning modules to help small business owners adopt AI into their operations. We know they want it, but often they don't know how to use it. They might be afraid that a changing regulatory landscape, for example, could negatively impact them down the road. They are afraid of giving up proprietary information. Can you talk more about the challenges small businesses are facing with this new technology, specifically if you are able to speak to it, and how it could potentially help them to compete for federal contracts? Ms. DINGLE. So we know that AI is being used in the evaluation process for federal contracts. So first of all, as a business owner, I need to understand how my proposals are being evaluated. So even having someone at the SBA or in one of the agencies be able to provide an informational session to tell us that or to have some educational programs. And I will use cybersecurity as an example. As the defense industrial base was--cybersecurity was rolled out, there were roadshows around the country to say, hey, this is what this is going to look like---Ms. SCHOLTEN. Yeah. Ms. DINGLE.--and here is how you need to be prepared. We need to be doing that now with AI. Right? So having some education for that might be really helpful. Making sure that the tools are accessible in terms of the cost associated with those tools. There has been some push to make sure that there are some cybersecurity tools that are available. Doing that same thing from an artificial intelligence standpoint would be really helpful. Ms. SCHOLTEN. Yeah. Ms. DINGLE. Business owners, they want to use the technology, but we are concerned, right? There is no real regulatory guidance on whether we can use AI as a part of our solution. There is no real guidance on what our exposure is with respect to privacy and loss of data for our clients. And so some assistance in that area would be great. Ms. SCHOLTEN. That is very, very helpful feedback. We teach our students, the first thing you learn in an English class is write for your audience, right? It is almost dystopian to think that that audience might be AI. But the reality is, we know that this is evaluating our proposals. And so making sure folks understand how to prepare that is critically important. We are teaching students now how to write smart AI prompts to get it to do what they want. You know, getting our small business owners prepared for drafting their proposals is a really good idea. We will follow up with your team. We would love to, you know, chat out some specifics there. Ms. DINGLE. Thank you. Ms. SCHOLTEN. My time is almost up, so I will yield back. That was very helpful. Thank you, Ms. Dingle. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentlelady yields back. I now recognize Mr. Patronis from the great state of Florida for 5 minutes. Mr. PATRONIS. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My district, northwest Florida, I have got over 100,000 veterans. I got 25,000 Active Duty, and it is definitely a stable part of the country because of their understanding, commitment to service, mission. But I think I am going to leave this kind of open for anybody that wants to chime in. What are we doing right and doing wrong? I know there are so many different organizations and groups that assemble to help those warfighters transition into careers, small business. But again, I am--I would rather you just, you know, throw darts at us where we are dropping the ball and creating problems to help those transitions, because there is--otherwise there wouldn't be so many different organizations trying to be the nonprofit solution, whether it be Operation New Uniform or what have you, that tries to help that. So I am, Mr. Chairman, I am open to any that wants to chime in. Mr. CLOSSON. Sure. So as somebody who transitioned you know, a while ago now, it has been 17 years, but being--having friends that are transitioning now and also working with Mission 22 and DAV and all of these agencies, these nonprofits trying to transition, is having these programs available within the military. Right? Because right now they are having to go out outside of that. There are--the military has done an amazing job from over the last couple of years of doing better transitioning. I was talking--we have a former colonel that works with Colossal now, and I was asking him because I was curious. He said it is getting better, right? And that there is a lot more care into that transition. But I think specifically around wanting to start an SDVOSB, a veteran-owned small business, a small business in general, are there classes available during that transition that they can point them in that direction and say--because a lot of it they train us to go get a job, right? Hey, this is what you need to do to go work for Lockheed or Raytheon or whoever else, and we are figuring that out. For me, when I made the decision just--there wasn't anything available. Right? Now, today, there are a lot of these programs like the DAV has of the SDVOSB veteran boot camp that they have, and there are these other agencies doing it. But my question is, is what is the government doing to foster that within the military? There may be some programs I am not sure about, so I don't want to say that that is not happening, but in the transitioning that I am hearing happening is we got to be there for them and be able to foster that. Mr. PATRONIS. Well, you have been there, done that. Okay. So in your career of service, when did you make up your mind that you were going to transition out? And ideally, what is the perfect timing to try to catch somebody with those transition procedures? Mr. CLOSSON. Absolutely. With me, it was, you know, when I got to Joint Base Andrews, I really got a better view of how the contractor can support the mission. And I was like, man, I think I could do this. Like, I really believe that I could bring value to this mission as a contractor and I can still serve the nation, right? Because I didn't want to take the uniform off, but I wanted to find a way to continue to serve. So in that transfer time is what I started doing is asking these companies I was working with as a military member, hey, how does this work? You know, I was just interviewing everyone. They probably thought I was crazy, but I knew that this is the path that I wanted to take, but there was nothing there for me. So the answer to your question is it is probably different with every member, right? But the reality is, is once that transition happens and you decide 6 months into it or a year into it, or you are hitting your 18 years and you are getting the itch and you got 2 left, is what programs are there to train them and to educate them on how to start an SDVOSB or veteran-owned small business? Mr. PATRONIS. Sure, sure. Mr. JAWOROWSKI. Yeah, I would add to that, I think that the programs that are there to support transitioning servicemembers into industry are great. We utilize them all the time. We hire from them frequently. When it comes to Active Duty internships, they frequently take place at the very tail end of the career, and if you have got somebody that, like Mr. Closson said, that has maybe got a few years left, that is a really good time to expose them to some of what industry has to offer, the challenges that industry faces, so they can make an informed decision about where they are going to take their future. I think that they can--the more--you know, rotation programs, maybe, you know, work with this company for a month and then a different company for a month, and they can see what the different size companies are really dealing with. I think that there is a lot of opportunity to improve there. Mr. PATRONIS. Sure. Ma'am? Ms. DINGLE. Thank you for your question. And might I add that doing those rotations would be really helpful for small businesses because we want that expertise. And I think that exposure for the folks that are still in will give them a sense of what the two environments look like because it can be pretty shocking to come out of the military or come out of federal service, like myself, and then transition into business. Mr. PATRONIS. Gotcha. Thank you. Mr. SCHWARTZ. Do I have time to answer? Oh, thank you. I will be very quick. Chairman WILLIAMS. You got 15 seconds. Mr. SCHWARTZ. Fifteen seconds. One of the things I think is very often overlooked is many veterans who leave the Department leave and they are like, I saw this problem, I know how to fix it in a way that other people don't. And that is something that I think we should really leverage when people leave. Like the company Onebrief that I mentioned earlier in the testimony, that person left the military and said, I saw this problem, I can fix it, and started a company to fix it. If we can capture that, we would really benefit. Mr. PATRONIS. Sure. Great answers. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentleman's time is up. Mr. PATRONIS. Thank you. Chairman WILLIAMS. I now recognize Mr. Jack from the great state of Georgia for 5 minutes. Mr. JACK. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. If I could start with Mr. Schwartz, I appreciate your testimony today, and I want to talk a little bit about, you know, you had a great graph that you included in your testimony that shows the declining number of companies contracting with the federal government, and would welcome your thoughts as to why you believe it is harder for small businesses to contract with the federal government, particularly within the defense industrial space. Mr. SCHWARTZ. So first, thank you for reading the written testimony. Appreciate it. I think there are a lot of challenges. Let me start with the workforce. Right? Is if you are a contracting officer and you have a lot of pressures and there is a perception of compliance that you have to do and you have to move fast, it is very difficult to sit back and say, okay, I can do this really fast or I can go slow, do more market research, figure out what the right companies are, who is offering the best thing, and find them. That go find them is hard because who knows about a small business? We had to find a plumber recently and we had no idea where to start except Roto-Rooter because they were right there. Right? They are easy. It is a lot harder to find some of these small businesses. I think that is one of the biggest challenges is the visibility or people knowing this is what they have to offer. Mr. JACK. You also included in your testimony the crushing burden of overregulation. Would welcome thoughts to this Committee as to how we as a Small Business Committee and a Republican majority can help reduce regulatory costs and burdens to small businesses trying to get involved. Mr. SCHWARTZ. Right. I will just review two. The first one is, as we were talking before, there are a number of small businesses that are subcontractors. And it is not infrequent that a requirement on a prime contractor is required to be flowed down through the contract to every lower tier, which means we are also putting those regulations on small businesses that are the subcontractors. Well, perhaps let's review those requirements of what has to go flow down and say, do we really need to flow that down? Is it really important? And related to that is systematically go through all of the regulations and say this was--this is a regulation because something that was passed in 1992. Do we really need it anymore or can we amend it to alleviate the burden? Mr. JACK. That is how I feel, too. Mr. Jaworowski, appreciate your testimony as well, and I would welcome for this Committee an answer to this question, because as a small business that does not have an SBA certification and must compete in the broader small business category, how challenging is it for those types of businesses to win awards? And do you believe you are at a disadvantage in terms of the contracts offered to you because of it? Mr. JAWOROWSKI. We are definitely at a disadvantage because the contract space and opportunity space for a company that is our size that doesn't apply for a set-aside that is set aside for socioeconomic basis forces us to compete at a higher level. And in my testimony, I talked about how there is this pool of companies that really punch above their weight. They are large businesses masquerading as small businesses that get to operate based on 8(a) criteria in similar spaces to us. So it is really a 300-person company going up against a behemoth that can be several thousand employees at times. So it is very, very challenging to find the right opportunity space. And frequently, if those companies that are large are pursuing a small business set-aside where we can compete, we often see contracting officers electing to do a direct award to an 8(a) rather than have a full-blown competition. The Rule of Two should apply there, but there is still subjectivity that can be applied to the Rule of Two, which can limit competition. Mr. JACK. Thank you. Next question, Mr. Closson, since we are talking about certificates, would welcome your opinion and perspective as to how the SDVOSB Certification has changed your ability to compete in the defense marketplace? Mr. CLOSSON. It has been extremely valuable. It has helped shape the company in every way. We started off just fighting any way that we could, but I think we hit it on two values that helped our grow. As they started setting aside for SDVOSB, we started working with the VA more and started getting some work there, and then started working with the Air Force, got a couple prime contracts, were awarded some GWACs that we are able to set aside, like SOOP and ITES, that have set aside requirements for SDVOSB. And, you know, also the large, you know, partners that we work with also have set aside standards within their large contracts. You just got to get to be out there and work as hard as you can and find the avenues. They don't run and punch you in the face. You got to go look for them and hunt them down through your relationships. But they are out there and we really hope to see more. Mr. JACK. Well, I appreciate you all's testimony today. With that, Mr. Chairman, I yield back. Chairman WILLIAMS. The gentleman yields back. And I would like to thank our witnesses today for your testimony and for appearing before us. It has been a great hearing. I hope when you go back home you can tell your friends that there are hearings that people don't yell and scream at. And there is a lot of--much of what we talked about, the Ranking Member and I were just talking about how much we agree from party to party on small businesses today. title: BUILDING AN AI-READY AMERICA: ADOPTING AI AT WORK
text: Today's hearing will examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping American workplaces and what that means for employers and employees. AI is no longer science fiction. It is here and there are already signs that it will significantly transform industries and workplaces. Optimistically, this technology may boost productivity, empower workers, and put the American Dream within reach for more Americans. We must also ensure that innovation and worker protections go hand in hand. To build an AI-ready America, we must first understand the AI technologies themselves, how employers are using these tools, and the potential risks AI adoption poses to workers. We want to help American workers and job creators to compete and succeed in an AI-driven economy. Today's hearing is a step in that direction. We will discuss today how the National Labor Relations Act can continue to protect worker rights and promote stable relationships between employees and management in the age of AI. As AI adoption grows, labor laws and their enforcement should strike the right balance between protecting workers and allowing innovation to spur job creation and business growth. This hearing will also discuss the critical role of data collection to gain understanding of AI's impact and to prepare workers. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) plays an important role in tracking workforce trends, and it can play an important role in collecting data on how AI is changing the modern workplace. Leveraging BLS insights will help us identify the challenges ahead and allow us to make evidence-based policy decisions. While technology can make our workplaces better, trust and transparency can benefit the workplace. When employers communicate openly about how AI is deployed, they protect rights, strengthen morale, and build trust. That trust is essential for a productive, competitive workforce, and for labor peace. The bottom line is that AI can create opportunity without compromising fairness or safety. We appreciate the insights our witnesses will offer about how we can ensure that innovation serves people--not the other way around. ______

text: HON. MORGAN LUTTRELL, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF TEXAS Mr. Luttrell. Mr. Chairman, Ranking Member, thank you for having me today. You both mentioned the importance of health. I am specifically going to speak on brain health, which I adamantly believe is something that we do not pay attention to, either in the medical space nationally or globally. As we move through these appropriations, I want to focus on the brain research innovative neurotechnologies through the NIH funding. Back in 2014, this was started. In 2014, I was exiting the military and actually in grad school studying neuroscience, and I did not specifically get to touch that grant funding, but I saw how it started to change the landscape. From 2014 to 2026, what we know about the brain and brain health has changed every second of every minute and every hour of every day. Currently, the 21st Century Cures Act, which provides funding for this program, is sunsetting, and of everything that we do in this wonderful place, one thing that we absolutely need to remember is how important that gelatinous substance between our ears is. It gives us capabilities. It allows us to do amazing things. It allows us--for you to understand what I am saying, contemplate the contemplation of thought, put a man on the moon, everything. If we had the ability to train and educate and cure the diseases of the brain, because we primarily focus from the neck down, and we have been doing that at an exceptional level since we have been walking around. Decreasing funding. I am actually asking for an increase in funding in this program, and this is the reason why. This place always asks for a return on the investment. It does, and if any program has provided or given the American people and the public something, it is this specific program, amongst many others, but this one specifically. It has provided brain mapping because today, currently, we still have no idea how this wonderful organism works. We just do not. We have not figured that out yet, but the scientists and researchers that are in this space have created brain mapping, neural pixels. They have given us the ability for deep brain stimulation. That directly affects Parkinson's disease. I have a family member who had Parkinson's, still does currently. Convulsions and shakes were out of control. Deep brain stimulation paused it. This money directly affects that, and because of the advancements of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and language models that live and breathe in laboratories and institutions of higher education, instead of baby steps, we are taking profound leaps forward. I had a traumatic brain injury when I was in the military, and I spent in the military and my post-military life addressing that issue, and it is the reason I went back to school. Having a pause, purposeful pause in these programs would kill a momentum that we will never get back. My professor said this was the decade of the brain, and that was 10 years ago. These computational analytics are allowing real-time diagnostics. We are able to see things at different levels inside the human brain. I have always been asked, why can we not figure this out? How can this be so challenging if we have been funding and doing these studies for decades? One of the many issues is, sir, your brain is different than mine. Young lady, yours is different than mine. Ma'am, yours is different than mine. You cannot have a control group of a thousand people because every single human brain is different, and you have to see it that way. That is one of the many challenges that our doctors, and clinicians, and scientists, and neuroscientists, and data scientists are facing, but they have got a lane and they are moving at amazing speed. In Washington, DC, I share this House with you. One thing, if we can get rid of something, we can add something. If we can do anything to help the American people, aside of that, if a mother brings her baby into the emergency room with a head injury, the neurologist can look at her and go, ``we have got this, I can give you your child back,'' because, currently, with brain disease and brain injury or brain distractions, we are dead in the water, and this program specifically is breaking through those barricades. text: Now one clear solution is through the strengthening of labor protections, a higher minimum wage, increased overtime threshold, and protected right to organize will be key to ensuring that AI benefits all of us, rather than making this gap, this gap here larger. My 32-hour work week proposal, my 32-hour work week bill, addresses the need for greater work protections in the new economy, the new American economy. Mr. Chairman, I yield back. Chairman Walberg. I thank the gentleman. I recognize now the gentlelady from Illinois, Ms. Miller. Ms. Miller. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. With how fast AI is developing, it is essential that Congress develop policies that promote educational opportunity, workforce and workforce development, while upholding user safety. It is also a matter of national security that the U.S. win the AI race. I appreciate the work that the Trump administration is doing, using AI to ensure students are prepared to enter the workforce while preventing it from being used for woke indoctrination. AI has become especially effective in the classroom, as it can personalize learning experiences while also helping students with special needs and learning disabilities. AI is equally beneficial to teachers as it helps create lesson plans, saving teachers hours of work per week. Over the course of a school year, this adds up to nearly 6 weeks of saved work time. AI is also beneficial to businesses and their employees, as it can teach valuable skills at a fraction of the cost. However, as AI continues to develop and progress, we must address how it may disrupt the job market, as well as teacherstudent relationships in the classroom. Mr. Khan, I am especially concerned about AI's effects on children concerning chatbots imitating human relationships. How can we address these issues while still using AI effectively in the classroom? Mr. Khan. Thank you for the question, Congresswoman. We share in your concern about the inappropriate relationship that a student could have with a chatbot in the classroom. The way that we guard against that is we make sure that any interaction with generative AI through our product and the way we believe all products should be used or AI products when used in schools, should be under the supervision of a teacher. Teachers have monitoring dashboards where they are flagged for inappropriate content, or maybe an inappropriate interaction that the child might be having in the experience. Then, of course, the experiences themselves are academically focused. They are not intended to create a relationship between a chatbot and a child. More importantly than that, certainly there are technology safeguards we put into the products. We equip teachers with understanding the risks that you just described. We help them before they even use this technology with their students in the classroom. They are introducing the technology with letting the child know about what this is, what this is not. This is not a companion. This is not something that you should be building a relationship with. Human connection is still the most important part of the educational process. The center of our work, you know, we have a slogan, it is teachers are magic, but that is very much the ethos of the company too, is that the greatest learning happens with the relationship of a teacher and a child, and a parent and a child. We keep that the center of our work, and only use AI to augment their ability to serve the needs of the children in the classroom and avoid the negative effects. Ms. Miller. I am glad that we agree on the danger that children could access that. I know in a school in Illinois recently, the kindergartners were working on a Chromebook and pornography just popped up on it. You know, we just need layer, layer, layer of protections, to make sure our kids' minds are protected. Mr. Khan. Absolutely. Ms. Miller. Okay. Then also for Ms. Nayak, how can Congress develop policies that will use AI to promote workforce development without sacrificing jobs? Ms. Nayak. Thank you, Congressman or Congresswoman, excuse me. We think that Congress should think about how all of the programs that already exist, unemployment programs, programs to help upskill and educate people, they should think about how those can also add AI skills into those trainings. What we are doing is we are providing a foundation of certifications. We are partnering with governments, we are partnering with employers to think about how those certifications can enter into their workflows, to think about how those certifications can lead to jobs. We would love to work with Congress to think about how our certifications could also be used in workforce development programs at the State level as well as federally. Ms. Miller. Would any of those certifications be available to students while they are still in high school, so that--OK. Ms. Nayak. Yes. That is our intention. Students, teachers, as well as the workforce. Ms. Miller. Okay, great. My final question is to Mr. Frazier. Oops. Well Chairman, you want me to finish? Chairman Walberg. 16 seconds. Ms. Miller. Can you talk more about needed safeguards for AI policy in light of student privacy? Mr. Frazier. Yes. First and foremost, very quickly I would say we also have to be attentive to the fact that today's AI is the worst AI we will ever use. If we want more AI tools to be safe and reliable in a student context, we also have to talk about updating and gathering student information. We cannot have one without the other. Better data leads to better AI. Ms. Miller. Thank you, and I yield back. Chairman Walberg. I thank the gentlelady, and I recognize the gentleman from Pennsylvania who is wondering how AI will help produce better whole milk. Chairman of the Ag Committee, Mr. Thompson. Mr. Thompson. I have got a lot of thoughts on that. Great applications in agriculture. Let us talk education today, which is a foundation of everything actually. Mr. Khan, you had reflected already on how K through 12 schools currently integrate AI-based assistive technology in the classrooms. I want to focus on students who are learning with various disabilities. What do you see as the, the opportunities there? You know we--you know, the reauthorization of the Individuals With Disabilities in Education Act is long overdue. Actually, this could be good timing. Mr. Khan. Thank you for the question, Congressman. As a former special education teacher, this is near and dear to my heart. AI can be an incredible assistive technology in supporting students with learning disabilities. Within our platform and many AI tools, one of the incredible advancements is in speech to text and text to speech. Often students with Individualized Education Programs, IEPs, students with disabilities will have a read aloud accommodation. AI can read aloud and in a natural voice that continues to have the child engaged in their education with a compelling narrator individually in the classroom, rather than having a teacher kneel down next to them to have to do that. Perhaps, you know, that is great for the individual child the teacher is with but, you know, when I was a special education teacher co-teaching, I could not get to every child in the classroom to give them that accommodation. There was a physical barrier for me to be able to, you know, implement the required accommodations that the children in the classroom that I was supporting had, and AI breaks down that barrier. It gives them the ability to have read aloud in the moments that they need it. In addition to that, when AI is informed with the needs of the child, especially when they are individualized needs that are state-mandated or federally mandated through an IEP, then the interaction that they have with the technology can be even more personalized to the needs that they have. Another example I might give is, you know, when I was teaching 9th grade English, there were students who were many grade levels behind in the class and students who are well advanced of their classmates. AI can give them personalized feedback across their ability levels if informed by their zone of proximal development. You know that that is the idea, that you do not want to give a child, you know, work that is so challenging that they disengage. You want to give them to them in a way that is like just stretches them just enough to help them grow to the next level, and AI can help get them into that zone of proximal development based on no matter where they started. When we can use the data that we have about kids and their needs, then AI can be something that increases the capacity of the educator to serve the diverse needs of the students in front of them in a way that has never been possible before. That gets me really inspired. Special education's probably the thing that, you know, is again near and dear to my heart, but also one of the most incredible ways that we can support the real needs of schools and districts right now. You know, special education is a designation, but every child learns differently, right? There are students who are multiple language learners in schools who can be served with this technology and translating in and out of English in their native language. There are so many incredible applications, for the specialized needs of learners in classrooms. Mr. Thompson. Very exciting, very exciting. Great for the kids, great for the teachers as well. Ms. Nayak, how is AI technology being integrated into workforce development to enhance skill acquisition and support career transitions? Ms. Nayak. Thank you, Congressman. We are seeing a lot of enterprises actually very excited for AI skill development. When we actually speak with our enterprises who are adopting our tools, one of the biggest things that they ask us for is actually certifications and skills-based training that they can provide to their workforce, so that they can leverage these AI tools. The way that it is being integrated is at OpenAI, we are partnering with enterprises to actually build out coursework and curriculum and certifications that will teach their workforce the skills that they believe that they need in order to be successful in their jobs in the AI era. Over the course of the next several months, we are going to be releasing several courses that we have built in partnership with these organizations. Mr. Thompson. Very good. How is AI being used at this point in career and technical education or CTE programs? Mr. Khan. CTE is a emergent use case in a really, really powerful way. We found that a lot of CTE educators are coming from industry. They are folks like my father, who are an HVAC technician, welders. They did not get a traditional training and education. They are learning how to use AI to lesson plan and build all of these really incredible resources where curriculum does not exist, to bring this technology in a way that helps folks build these working class or whatever I would call living wage jobs, right? They are getting access to these living way jobs, and the teachers of those jobs can actually learn how to be a teacher a lot faster, because they are able to utilize this technology to build things like lesson plans as nontraditionally educated educators. Mr. Thompson. Very good. Well, thank you. My time's expired. I call them essential workers actually. Chairman Walberg. I thank the gentleman. Now since we have discussed AI with whole milk, I suppose we ought to discuss AI's impact on bourbon. Mr. Thompson. Absolutely. Chairman Walberg. I recognize a gentleman from Kentucky, Mr. Comer. Mr. Comer. Well, thank you Mr. Chairman, and I thank our witnesses for being there today. I am very excited about what AI could mean for my district in rural Kentucky. In my congressional district in Paducah, Kentucky, a former Department of Energy site that once supported nuclear weapons production is now being redeveloped for advanced energy projects and AI data center uses alongside uranium enrichment facilities. Just last week, I am very happy to announce that one company in Paducah received a $900 million task order from the Department of Energy to enrich uranium and power America's nuclear future. At the same time, local workers are preparing to reskill and upskill to meet the needs of companies reindustrializing the Paducah Department of Energy site. For a lot of folks back home, this isn't theatrical. This is--it is about whether they can save their communities and move into good well-paying jobs as technology changes. Paducah and the surrounding communities in west Kentucky have a skilled workforce built around energy manufacturing and national security, and they're now being asked to transition into this next generation of infrastructure. I see this as a real opportunity for Kentucky to be a part of the future of AI, not left behind. Ms. Nayak, how do you see AI-driven industries creating new kinds of jobs in places like Paducah, Kentucky? Ms. Nayak. Thank you, Congressman, and I think Paducah is a really exciting example for how AI could actually move with industries and kind of transition them over time. I think the example that you gave of data centers and being able to leverage their skills to power the next generation of this technology is a very exciting one. What we are doing with the jobs and certifications effort is we are actually leveraging our AI foundations courses to build curriculum for specific industries like the ones in your district, to enable them to actually gain the AI skills, but also leverage the skills that they already have in this new era. We are very excited to see that enabling workers to actually transition with the times and then actually lead to much more economic growth and new industries or industries that are just transitioning with AI. Mr. Comer. Well, that is great, and we talk about it a lot in this Committee and I think we are all in a majority agreement, that it is a new type of job training in America. I guess Ms. Nayak, what specific kinds of training or specific certifications would help average workers that want to re-skill move more quickly into these new types of jobs? How does OpenAI think about supporting those pathways? Ms. Nayak. Congressman, we are investing in several different styles of courses that will lead to an OpenAI certification. Our first one is something that we think can be valuable to everyone from a teacher to a student to a worker, which is AI Foundations, which teaches them how to use tools like ChatGPT, teaches them how to build agentic workflows and then also teaches them how to bring their community along and actually train the trainer and teach others around them to use AI. That is our kind of first set of courses, and we are already starting to roll those out. We will finish that full curriculum series this month. The second set of courses are focused on AI builders. Those are the ones who are technologists or even, like the examples that you give, who are operating data centers or operating energy facilities, where they are actually leveraging AI to build tools for others to use. We are going to start to build out an AI builders curriculum and coursework that will empower those individuals to be able to use our tools. Over time, we see that we would love to partner with every industry to think about how we can take those types of courses and then adapt them to their industries. Examples of that is we have already released a AI teacher course, which takes our AI Foundations course and actually augments it and implements it for teachers. We are hoping to do that in the health care space as well. We think it is very exciting. We think that this foundational curriculum can lead to a lot of benefit for many different industries. Mr. Comer. Well, thank you very much for your insight. I am very eager, Mr. Chairman, to see how AI can unleash workforce development opportunities for my constituents in Kentucky. Thank you all again for being here. Mr. Chairman, look forward to working with the Committee to see that we can achieve this goal of retraining a new workforce to be able to quickly adapt into the bright future that AI has. With that, I yield back. Chairman Walberg. I thank the gentleman. I now recognize the gentleman from Guam, Mr. Moylan. Mr. Moylan. Chairman Walberg and Ranking Member Scott, thanks for hosting today's important hearing and thank you today to our panel for providing your expertise. The rapid advancement of AI deployment through the workforce and schools and it is provided untapped opportunities, of course. While we have an unlimited potential, we should also be cautious about irresponsible use and the threats of our adversarial nations, what they can pose with the new technology. That is why I work consistently with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to ensure that appropriate guardrails and strategic planning are in place to generate jobs, ensure AI dominance and protect our Nation and its people. Ms. Nayak, oftentimes certain areas can be left behind in innovative workforce development. To maintain America AI leadership across the globe and in all corners of the country, what approaches can ensure that no community is left behind, particularly in the territories, rural areas and remote locations where AI applications can solve critical infrastructure, logistics and economic development problems? Ms. Nayak. Thank you, Congressman. We share in your concern that AI could leave people behind or it could actually help to accelerate rural communities or communities that normally wouldn't be reached by technology. We are hopeful that it will be the latter. What you are talking about is something we call the capability overhang, where we want to make sure that people can actually use AI to its fullest and we need to be able to skill them to be able to do so. What we are doing here at OpenAI is a couple of things. One is we are leveraging certifications and those certifications are available on ChatGPT. Really anyone could access them. The beauty of that is that with ChatGPT as well, you could actually personalize a course toward different communities. You mentioned territories. You could actually take a course and you could translate it to different languages or, you know, different levels of education or understanding. I think that that will actually make this more adaptable, so that it can actually be personalized to those communities rather than something that's only focused on kind of urban areas in the U.S. Mr. Moylan. Thank you for that. Also, another question for you. As AI transforms professionals like finance services, supply chain management and healthcare, what mechanisms would you recommend for enabling colleges and universities to rapidly redesign programs and deploy industry, recognize credentials that meet immediate workforce needs while students and families are demanding these changes? Ms. Nayak. Thank you, Congressman. We have been working quite a bit with universities, not only kind of large universities but also community colleges. We have been talking to them a lot about how we could leverage our certification programs within those universities. One way is that we actually need to skill up the professors and teachers in those universities. We are building coursework for those teachers to actually understand how do you build AI-based curriculum. That is part one. Part two is we are building coursework for students. Right now, we have a student AI lab, where as we are building this course curriculum we are actually having that lab give us feedback, both positive and negative, as to how it is actually helping them, where we are actually missing the mark. That has been super useful for us in developing this course, to make sure that it actually applies to our students and universities. Then third, we are also working with enterprises, so that they can tell us where they are seeing the biggest gaps and then ideally, we can take that back to the universities and community colleges and actually partner with them to close those gaps. We really see this as a virtuous loop, and we are excited that AI can actually help create and connect that loop in ways we never saw before. Mr. Moylan. That is terrific. Going on that line with the commercial enterprises, how can Federal policy support small and medium sized businesses, local governments and public institutions like schools and public health systems, in adopting AI tools and upscaling existing workforces, particularly where expertise and training is limited? Ms. Nayak. Thank you, Congressman. We are actually seeing that around 40 percent of small businesses are already reporting using AI today, and the majority of small businesses actually see this technology as increasingly important to their industries. We are actually very excited about the impact that this could have on small businesses from, you know, businesses that could not afford to have specific services, where they were kind of stringing together work themselves, now maybe they could use AI to augment it so that they have to spend less time doing things that they don't love and spend more time building their business. What we are doing here is again with the certifications effort, we want to give small businesses the tools to be able to adopt AI really rapidly and to be able to prevent that capability gap, so that they can actually use it to increase their businesses. Mr. Moylan. Thank you so much. Thank you to the panel. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Chairman Walberg. I thank the gentleman. I recognize the very patient gentleman from Virginia, the Ranking Member Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Ms. Givens, we have talked about bias and you mentioned guidance on websites from Federal agencies. Can you say a word about the status of that guidance? Ms. Reeve Givens. Absolutely, and it comes up in both of the topics of today's hearing. In the hiring and employment space, over the past 5 years the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Department of Justice, Department of Labor and National Labor Relations Board did extensive work to put out guidance for employers and workers about how to use AI in a way that complies with existing employment laws. Unfortunately, all of those pieces of guidance have been removed from their websites. I do provide links to them in my written testimony from people who preserved that record. Unfortunately, that pullback is just a very troubling sign about the leadership those agencies are showing right now for workers and employers. In the education space, I will just note that the Department of Education, through its Office of Education Technology and the Office of Civil Rights, also put out very important guidance on how to ensure the use of AI in education spaces complies with existing civil rights laws. It is important that that continues to be available to people as well. Mr. Scott. Thank you. Can you, on that discrimination guide, discrimination cases, can you talk about the importance of disparate impact analysis? Ms. Reeve Givens. Yes. One of the foundational tenets of our civil rights laws is acknowledging that one form of discrimination can best be captured through assessing the disparate impact that it has on protected populations or people based on their protected characteristics in our society. If that protection is removed, then anybody who is trying to say they have been treated unfairly under the law has to make a very difficult case about what was in the mind of the person that hired 99 percent white people into their workforce, just to give one example. That is incredibly difficult to do, and it ends up essentially making our laws almost impossible to enforce. Disparate impact for a long time has been a tenet of how we actually address inequality in these key features of people's lives, and making sure that people with protected characteristics, that they are not being judged on that basis, but on their ability to contribute to a job in question. Mr. Scott. If a businessman has off the shelf software that turns out to be discriminatory, who is responsible for--who is accountable for the discrimination? Ms. Reeve Givens. Under the law, the employer is. Right now, it is difficult to bring those cases because of the lack of transparency and visibility into how those tools are affecting the workforce, which is why we need not only enforcement of existing law, but also additional protections provided by Congress to have there be more transparency and testing in when these tools are used and deployed. Mr. Scott. In professional development, are there problems we need to be sensitive to in providing professional development with AI, rather than the industry providing itself if there is embedded bias in the software? Ms. Reeve Givens. I think in any tasking and other training materials, it is important to think about what is being taught and the quality of what is being taught. One hopes that that is the hallmark of effective learning and effective teaching materials. One of the areas we have been focused on in the ed tech space is how to make sure that ed tech vendors, just to give one example, are much more transparent about their grounding in learning science, so that teachers, educators, school administrators can be making informed decisions when they turn to these tools and are asking not only how are you trained, what is the science, but also how are you evaluating your impact over time? Some are starting to do this, but the paperwork around it, the disclosures, the standards, as Mr. Khan was saying, are not there yet and it is an important area to focus on right now. Mr. Scott. Thank you. Mr. Frazier, you pointed out the importance of collecting data. You did not say what data we needed to be collecting on. Mr. Frazier. In 72 seconds, I think that there is a tremendous need to focus on adoption, what tools are being adopted, focusing on the intensity and novelty of that adoption. Not only do you have access to a tool, but how are you using it and in what ways are you using it? Then I also think we also need to pay attention to which tools are explicitly being used in which institutional settings, getting an understanding of whether a company, for example, is using last year's iteration of a certain model or the latest technology can give us real insights as well. It is really an extensive effort that has to be maintained, to get a true picture of how AI is diffusing across society. It is one we must pursue if we want better policy. Mr. Scott. Let me try to get another question in. Florida has a proposed AI bill of rights for Florida. Can you say whether or not it is important for states to control the situation or Federal Government? Then, while you say that executive orders do not override State laws, statutes do, is that right? Mr. Frazier. That is correct under the supremacy clause, that Federal law can overrule State laws that conflict with it. I would say also that in the domain of AI, states have a very real and very acknowledged role in governing AI use cases by end users. If and when we see states try to regulate beyond their own borders, however, that infringes upon our Federalist system in which Congress, you all, are tasked with governing interState matters. Mr. Scott. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Chairman Walberg. I thank the gentlemen. I thank the--the panel. I hope you noticed the extent of the numbers of members on both sides of the aisle that showed great interest in making time to leave other committees, et cetera and be here to ask questions. This is something that we will continue as well. Thank you, each of you, for sharing your expertise and we know where to find you if we need more answers. I now would recognize the Ranking Member for his closing remarks. Mr. Scott. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I would first ask unanimous consent for a report from the Economic Policy Institute entitled ``Unbalanced labor market power is what makes technology, including AI, threatening to workers. The best AI policy to protect workers is boosting their bargaining position.'' Chairman Walberg. Without objection. [The report of Mr. Scott follows:] [GRAPHICS NOT AVAILABLE IN TIFF FORMAT]
